etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English what, from Old English hwæt (“what”), from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat (“what”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷód (“what”), neuter form of *kʷós (“who”). Cognate with Scots whit (“what”), North Frisian wat (“what”), Saterland Frisian wat (“what”), West Frisian wat (“what”), Dutch wat (“what”), Low German wat (“what”), German was (“what”), Danish hvad (“what”), Norwegian Bokmål hva (“what”), Swedish vad (“what”), Norwegian Nynorsk kva (“what”), Icelandic hvað (“what”), Latin quod (“what, which”).

definitions.definition: (interrogative) Which, especially which of an open-ended set of possibilities.
(exclamative) Used to form exclamations indicating that something is remarkable, in either a good or bad way.

quote.citation: Little Red Riding Hood, traditional folk tale
quote.text: “Oh Granny, what big eyes you have,” said Little Red Riding Hood.

definitions.definition: Emphasises that something is noteworthy or remarkable in quality or degree, in either a good or bad way; may be used in combination with certain other determiners, especially 'a', less often 'some'.
(interrogative) Which thing, event, circumstance, etc.: used in asking for the specification of an identity, quantity, quality, etc.

quote.text:
The gym is across from … what? — The gym is across from the lounge. — Across from the lounge. Right. Thanks!
Audio (US):(file)

definitions.definition: (fused relative) That which; those that; the thing(s) that.
(fused relative) Anything that; all that; whatever.

quote.citation: 1902, J. M. Barrie, The Admirable Crichton:
quote.text: That’s her; that’s the thing what has stole his heart from me.
For, it is a name what strikes fear in the heart of anyone what hears it.

definitions.definition: (interrogative) In what way; to what extent.

Used before a prepositional phrase to emphasise that something is taken into consideration as a cause or reason; usually used in combination with 'with' (see what with), and much less commonly with other prepositions.

quote.citation: 1787, Henry St. John, Lord Viscount Bolingbroke, Letters on the Study and Use of History: A Letter to Sir William Windham, page 83:
quote.text: In short; what by the indiscretion of people here, what by the rebound which came often back from London, what by the private interests and ambitious views of persons in the French court, and what by other causes unnecessary to be examined now, the most private transactions came to light [...]

quote.citation: 1815, Rev. Mr. Milne, letter reprinted in The Evangelical Magazine and Missionary Chronicle, Volume 23, page 82. [1]
quote.text: The Chinese of all ranks, and in every place, received my books gladly, and listened with patience to what I had to say about the true God.—So that what from opportunities of attending to the object of my Mission among the Chinese—what from seasons of religious instruction to Dutch and English—what from intercourse with gentlemen of education and knowledge of the world—what from occasions of stating clearly the object of Missions, and of endeavouring to remove prejudices against them—and what from the view of a highly cultivated country, happy under an enlightened and liberal government, I have much reason to be satisfied with this journey [...]

definitions.definition: An expression of surprise or disbelief.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: What, have his daughters brought him to this pass?

definitions.definition: What do you want? An abrupt, usually unfriendly enquiry as to what a person desires.
(British, colloquial, dated) Clipping of what do you say? Used as a type of tag question to emphasise a statement and invite agreement, often rhetorically.

quote.citation: 1918, Denis Garstin, The Shilling Soldiers‎[2], London: Hodder and Stoughton, page 83:
quote.text: “That’s riled them,” said my compaion. “Good work, what?”

quote.citation: 1991 May 12, “Kidnapped!”, in Jeeves and Wooster, Series 2, Episode 5:
quote.text: Chuffy: WHAT? No, no, no, no, no. My casa is your casa, what?

definitions.definition: What did you say? I beg your pardon? This usage is often considered impolite, with the more polite "Pardon?" or "Excuse me?" preferred.
Indicating a guess or approximation, or a pause to try to recall information.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book VI, Canto IX”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 7:
quote.text: They prayd him sit, and gave him for to feed / Such homely what as serves the simple clowne, / That doth despise the dainties of the towne […]

definitions.definition: (countable) The identity of a thing, as an answer to a question of what.

quote.citation: 2005, Norman K. Denzin, Yvonna S. Lincoln, The SAGE Handbook of Qualitative Research, page 493:
quote.text: The emphasis on the interplay between the hows and whats of interpretive practice is paramount.

definitions.definition: (countable) Something that is addressed by what, as opposed to a person, addressed by who.

quote.citation: 2012, "We Are Both", season 2, episode 2 of Once Upon a Time
quote.text:
Regina: What are you?
Rumplestiltskin: What? What? What? My, my, what a rude question! I am not a what.
